Suppose that for each \(C_j\) there is a nonempty designated hub set \(H_j\subseteq C_j\), with \(h_j=|H_j|\le4\), such that:

1. Every direction \(i\in C_j\setminus H_j\) has a globally fixed unary rule
\[
f_i(x)=a_i+\lambda_i x_{p(i)},\qquad
a_i,\lambda_i\in\mathbb F_2,\quad p(i)\in H_j.
\tag{CH-C1}
\]
In particular these leaf rules do not vary with assignments to preceding components.

2. For each such \(i\), all hub-direction edge-color functions \(f_h\), \(h\in H_j\setminus\{p(i)\}\), are independent of \(x_i\). A hub can depend arbitrarily on its own leaves, other hub bits, and earlier-component bits. No hub may read a leaf assigned to another hub.

Put \(\beta_1=\beta_2=2\), \(\beta_3=4\), and \(\beta_4=2\).

**Theorem (owner-local SCC cross-seam lifting).** Under these hypotheses,
\[
\boxed{|P(f)|\ge\prod_{j=1}^{t}\beta_{h_j}>0.}
\tag{CH-C2}
\]
For components with four hubs the theorem uses the previously certified unrestricted \(Q_4\) favorable-root minimum of nine; for up to three hubs it uses the corresponding \(Q_1,Q_2,Q_3\) bounds. It is enough that conditions (CH-C1) and (2) hold componentwise; the hub functions may change arbitrarily with preceding bits.

*Proof.* Suppose we have selected a paired starting root on the previously processed components and its rising and falling full witness paths. They have possibly different zero-to-one seam states in earlier directions. Condition on these two earlier seam states to obtain two colorings of the next component. Their hub functions may differ, but by (CH-C1) their leaf functions agree and remain unary in their designated reader hub. Condition (2) gives owner-local independence in both conditional colorings.

Apply the corrected owner-local cross-hub lifting theorem to these two conditional colorings. The rising hub coloring with all leaves fixed to zero and the falling hub coloring with all leaves fixed to one each have at least \(a_h\) favorable hub roots, where \(a_1=2,\ a_2=3,\ a_3=6,\ a_4=9\). By inclusion-exclusion their opposite-orientation root sets intersect in at least \(2a_h-2^h\) hub roots: respectively \(2,2,4,2\). Each such hub root extends to one common starting root of the two component paths.

Insert the rising component path at the zero-to-one seam of the earlier rising witness and the falling component path at that of the earlier falling witness. Colors of earlier directions are independent of later bits by the condensation ordering, and the component paths use the new directions once each. Hence the full resulting paths remain monotone and share the same combined starting root. Distinct hub roots produce distinct extensions, and extensions of distinct earlier roots remain distinct. Inducting over the component order proves (CH-C2). \(\square\)

**Construction.** With the SCC decomposition and designated owner-local unary rules supplied, one paired root and two witness orders can be found using \(O(N)\) direction-edge evaluations and \(O(N^2)\) elementary operations. Tabulate the hub colorings on at most four bits at the two earlier seam states, enumerate hub roots and orders to find a cross-favorable hub root, choose each leaf's starting bit by the two-case owner-local lemma, and topologically sort the monotone phase-compatible precedence constraints. Only a bounded number of hub-edge evaluations is needed per component and at most two unary leaf evaluations per nonhub direction. Updating explicit witness orders by insertion takes \(O(N^2)\) list operations. This construction does not include discovery of the influence digraph from an oracle.

**Scope and correction.** The theorem does not cover arbitrary three- or four-hub stars. In particular merely having globally fixed unary reader rules for nonhubs, or only three branching vertices in a strongly connected component, is insufficient for the owner-local proof: nonlinear hub functions might read a leaf assigned to a different hub. The previous unrestricted CH2 statement and its unrestricted constructive corollary are withdrawn as unsupported by that argument. This qualification leaves the separately proved one-feedback and two-hub-star results intact.


#### Permutation-reader SCC closure with variable predecessor conditions

**Theorem.** Let F color the undirected edges of Q_N. Assume every strongly connected component C of the directed influence graph either satisfies a previously proved positive cross-favorable criterion, or has three hubs h_0,h_1,h_2 and three fixed disjoint nonhub groups L_0,L_1,L_2, with arbitrary multiplicities. At each fixed assignment y of preceding-component bits, require that all leaves w in L_i obey
\[
F^y_w(z)=z_{h_{\sigma_y(i)}}+a_{i,y}\pmod2,
\tag{CPS1}
\]
where the reader assignment \(\sigma_y\) is **any permutation** of the three hubs and the offsets \(a_{i,y}\) are arbitrary. Both the permutation and offsets may change with y. Hub edge functions are unrestricted nonlinear functions of every other internal bit and may also change with y.

Then F has a paired root. In particular every antipodally odd coloring on Q_(N+1) with such a lower-facet coloring has a monochromatic full antipodal geodesic, regardless of bridge-edge colors.

*Proof.* Process the directed SCCs in topological order. At any step choose rising and falling geodesics from a common root in the processed prefix, with seam states y_0 and y_1. The next block's conditional colorings F^{y_0} and F^{y_1} satisfy the full permutation-reader cross theorem (PRH2), even when their reader permutations, offsets, and nonlinear hub tables differ. They therefore admit rising and falling full block geodesics from a common block root. Insert each block path into the respective prior seam. Previous edge colors ignore future block bits, so neither path's earlier colors change. Each enlarged path remains monotone and uses all directions once. Repeat for all components; the other allowed component classes use their previously established cross-root lemmas. Apply the free-bridge equivalence to obtain the final statement. \(\square\)

**Constructive form.** Given the SCC decomposition and reader assignments, each three-hub block can be solved using at most 192 evaluations of the two conditional hub-edge truth tables: clone-contract its leaf groups to one representative each, add any absent dummy groups, enumerate roots and orders in the resulting Q_6 core, and lift the chosen paths by consecutive leaf duplication. Across all components this gives O(N) edge-color evaluations and O(N^2) elementary list operations, exclusive of finding the SCC decomposition from an arbitrary black-box coloring.

**Boundary.** Reader maps with repeated hub assignments, or leaf offsets varying within a fixed group, are not covered. This all-dimensional component theorem uses a computer-assisted six-cube core but does not invoke the earlier refuted unrestricted hub-to-leaf polarization lemma.

#### Paired-root enumeration of unary functional influence

Let f be a binary edge coloring of Q_n in which each direction i is constant or of the form \(f_i=x_{p(i)}+\epsilon_i\pmod2\), with p(i) different from i. Its directed influence graph has indegree at most one. Let the directed cycles have lengths \(\ell_1,\ldots,\ell_t\). For a starting root x put \(\alpha_i=x_{p(i)}+\epsilon_i\) on each cycle.

**Theorem.** The root x belongs to \(P(f)\) if and only if the bits alpha_i are nonuniform on every directed reader cycle. Consequently
\[
\boxed{|P(f)|=2^{n-\sum_j\ell_j}\prod_{j=1}^t(2^{\ell_j}-2)
\ge2^{n-\tau(D(f))}.}\tag{UF1}
\]
Equality in the feedback multiplicity inequality holds precisely when every directed cycle has length two. If all directions are readers, a paired root supports monochromatic full geodesics of both colors.

*Proof.* If alpha is constant, say a, on one reader cycle, the earliest cycle step in any order sees its parent unflipped and has color a, while the latest sees its parent flipped and has color 1-a. Thus a=0 rules out falling geodesics and a=1 rules out rising geodesics. Such a root cannot be paired.

Otherwise, for either chosen color b impose that p(i) precede i in each cycle precisely when alpha_i+b=1. Nonuniform alpha guarantees that these constraints are not a directed cycle. A topological order makes every cycle step color b. Combine separate reader-cycle components, choosing color zero on all cycles for rising paths and color one for falling paths. Constant-source components are inserted in the appropriate monotone color phase. Attach every noncycle reader direction outward from its parent: because its edge color toggles when the parent is crossed, insert its direction immediately before or after the parent's step to match the parent step color. This does not modify previous direction colors; each initial new bit is arbitrary. Therefore both monotone paths start from the same root and the criterion is sufficient. When every component contains a reader cycle, choose the same monochromatic color throughout to obtain two monochromatic witnesses.

Each reader cycle admits 2^ell initial assignments, just two of which yield uniform alpha; all noncycle bits are free. This gives (UF1). The cycles are disjoint, so their number is tau(D). Each factor 2^ell-2 is at least 2^(ell-1), with equality only for ell=2. QED.

Independently verified over every signed-reader Q3 and Q4 coloring, every mixed constant/reader Q2--Q4 coloring, and random Q5--Q6 colorings (nori_signed_reader_roots_audit.py and nori_mixed_functional_roots_audit.py).


#### Conditional three-hub SCC closure for arbitrary reader maps

The three-group cross-root theorem (NM5) removes the bijectivity requirement from the earlier conditional permutation-reader SCC argument.

**Theorem (unrestricted map selection at every seam).** Let F be an ordinary binary coloring of Q_N, and order the strongly connected components of its directed influence graph topologically. Suppose each component is either already covered by a previously established positive conditional cross-root theorem, or has three hubs \(h_0,h_1,h_2\) and three fixed disjoint nonhub groups \(L_0,L_1,L_2\), of arbitrary sizes, with the following property. For every assignment \(y\) of earlier-component bits, all leaves \(w\in L_i\) satisfy
\[
\boxed{F^y_w(z)=z_{h_{\rho_y(i)}}+a_{i,y}\pmod2,}\tag{RSC1}
\]
where \(\rho_y:\{0,1,2\}\to\{0,1,2\}\) is **any** map, not necessarily injective, and \(a_{i,y}\) are arbitrary signs uniform within each group. The three hub-edge functions of each conditional coloring may depend nonlinearly on all other component bits and arbitrarily on preceding bits.

Then F has a paired root. In particular every antipodally odd coloring of Q_(N+1) whose selected N-facet satisfies this hypothesis has a monochromatic full antipodal geodesic, for any legal perpendicular bridge coloring.

*Proof.* Maintain rising and falling full geodesics from a common root on the already processed SCC prefix. Their monotone phase seams may be at different prefix vertices y_0,y_1. The conditional colorings F^{y_0},F^{y_1} on the next component have the same fixed leaf groups, but can have entirely different maps \(\rho_{y_0},\rho_{y_1}\), offsets, and nonlinear hub functions. By (NM5), they have a common starting component root supporting rising and falling full component geodesics. Insert those geodesics into the two prefix seams. Earlier-direction edge colors are independent of later-component bits by the topological order, so the resulting full paths preserve their colors and use each direction once. Induction yields a paired root. Other allowed component types use their previously proved cross-root criteria. The free-bridge equivalence transfers the paired root to a monochromatic antipodal geodesic in the larger odd coloring. \(\square\)

**Constructive consequence.** With the decomposition, three group assignments, and conditional reader rules supplied, a root and both witnessing direction orders can be constructed using O(N) edge-color evaluations and O(N^2) order-list operations. At each stage contract a representative leaf of each nonempty group (add dummy leaves for absent groups), tabulate both six-dimensional conditional hub models using at most 192 hub-edge evaluations, and enumerate 64 roots and 720 orders to locate a cross-root. Expand each selected leaf step consecutively across its group and insert the two component orders into the previous seams. The constant six-dimensional search is warranted by the computer-assisted theorem. Discovering the influence graph from unrestricted black-box data is excluded from the stated query complexity.

**Limit.** This settles the global SCC branch with any three-group signed reader maps, even if all three groups read the same hub at one seam and three different hubs at the other. It does not handle arbitrarily many distinct joint leaf types or nonlinear multi-hub leaf rules, and it does not close unrestricted NORI1.


#### Rooted phase signatures and omission rigidity under one-way extensions

Let c be any binary undirected-edge coloring of Q_n. Adjoin r dummy directions y, retaining original colors c_i(x) independently of y, and assign each dummy direction j an arbitrary color f_j(x) depending only on the original vertex x, independently of all dummy bits. For a root x and integer k>=1, let M_k(c,x) be the greatest length of a direction-simple path beginning at x with at most k color changes. Let O_k(c,x) be the family of sets of omitted original directions for paths attaining M_k(c,x). Then for every dummy root y, M_k(C,(x,y))=r+M_k(c,x), and O_k(C,(x,y))=O_k(c,x). In particular every maximum path in C traverses all r dummy directions, and the old-direction omission spectrum is unchanged. The same holds separately for path words with colors 0-star-1-star and 1-star-0-star. Proof: projecting away dummy steps gives the upper bound and shows every maximum extension projects to a maximum source path. Conversely choose any source maximum path. If it has a color change, pause at one such transition vertex v, traverse all dummy edges of the old color and then all dummy edges of the next color; the dummy colors f_j(v) remain fixed because dummy steps do not change x. This inserts every dummy edge without adding a change. For a monochromatic path, insert dummy edges at its beginning or end, grouped by color, requiring at most one change. Both groups retain the prescribed monotone color-word orientation as appropriate. Thus every source maximal omission set lifts and no additional omission set arises. For r=1 this holds for every undirected coloring of the new edges, because such a color is necessarily independent of its own new bit. Rootwise favorable full-geodesic sets of a single dummy extension consequently factor as the source favorable-root set times Q_1. If a hypothetical minimum-dimension coloring of Q_n had no full one-change geodesic, every codimension-one facet would have a full one-change path by minimality, so its maximum one-change paths would omit each of the n directions in some example. Therefore changing which single dummy direction survives in an independent double cannot give an obstruction based solely on globally omitted direction sets; an additional constraint relating roots or opposite facets would be needed.

MINIMAL-COUNTEREXAMPLE SATURATION. Suppose c is a hypothetical minimum-dimensional arbitrary binary cube-edge coloring of Q_n with no full one-change antipodal geodesic. Every restriction of c to either facet omitting direction i is then a coloring of Q_(n-1) with a full one-change geodesic. Thus L_1(c)=n-1 and every singleton {i}, i in [n], occurs as the omission set of some maximum one-change path of c. In its independent double c box c, maximum length equals 2n-2. Every cross-block pair {i,n+j} occurs as the omission set of a maximum one-change path, by choosing paths in a facet omitting i in the first factor and in a facet omitting j in the second, reversing path orientations as needed and interleaving their zero and one portions. Conversely the factor projection bounds demand that every maximum product path omit one direction in each block, so the complete omission family of global maxima is { {i,n+j} : i,j in [n] }, of cardinality n^2. Every (2n-1)-face of the product contains a maximum product path as well. Therefore even complete coverage of every admissible two-direction omission pair across longest paths does not imply a one-change spanning geodesic. A dimension-deletion strategy must exploit rooted endpoint, phase-seam or inter-layer color dependence, not omission supports alone.

ROOTED PHASE-SIGNATURE FACTORIZATION. For root x in c and an oriented word 0-star-1-star, define S(c;x) as the family of ordered disjoint direction sets (A,B) for which there exists a direction-simple path rooted at x, traversing precisely A during its zero phase and B during its one phase. Empty phases are allowed. The transition vertex is x xor A and the endpoint is x xor A xor B. For independent product colorings c box d, with disjoint direction labels, the entire rooted signature family factorizes: S(c box d;(x,y)) = { (A union A', B union B') : (A,B) in S(c;x), (A',B') in S(d;y) }. Necessity follows by projecting any global 0-star-1-star path onto the two blocks; sufficiency follows by interleaving both zero prefixes first and both one suffixes afterward. The analogous formula holds with colors reversed. Hence rooted oriented maximum lengths satisfy M_up(c box d;(x,y)) = M_up(c;x)+M_up(d;y), and likewise for M_down. Unoriented rooted maximum length is the maximum of these two phasewise sums; unlike global maximum lengths it need not equal the sum of the two unoriented rooted maxima. The sets of attainable transition vertices and attainable omitted direction sets likewise factor under a fixed oriented phase and fixed optimal length. This proves that the full switch-vertex signature information in an independent product carries no cross-block correlation: deletion based only on its two phase direction sets cannot enforce an exchange between factors.

SMALL-DIMENSION AUDIT. For randomized undirected edge colorings on factor cubes of dimensions (1,2),(2,2),(2,3),(3,3), rooted feasible signature families were enumerated by exhaustive direction-subset dynamic programming and agreed with their Cartesian products at every root. Separate randomized checks verified the rooted one-way extension identity and its omission spectrum for source dimensions through five and several multi-dummy extensions.

#### Minimal-counterexample feedback and axis-face restrictions

STRONGLY CONNECTED MINIMAL-COUNTEREXAMPLE REDUCTION. In a binary edge coloring c of Q_n, draw a directed influence arc j->i when the i-edge color function changes under toggling bit j at some vertex. Suppose a nonempty proper set R has no incoming influence from its complement S, so all R-edge colors are independent of S-bits. If the R-coloring admits a full 0-star-1-star geodesic and every induced S-coloring at a frozen R-vertex admits some full 0-star-1-star geodesic, then c admits a full 0-star-1-star geodesic: run the R zero prefix, insert a full S zero-then-one path at its transition vertex, and finish the R one suffix. The S root can be chosen after the R transition vertex is fixed, and R steps do not read S-bits. In particular, a hypothetical minimum-dimensional counterexample to existence of an unrestricted full one-change geodesic must have a strongly connected directed influence graph. Otherwise choose a source strongly connected component R and use the minimality hypothesis on R and each conditional S-coloring, both lower-dimensional, to construct the full geodesic. This strengthens the elementary fact that a minimal counterexample cannot have a dummy-like sink direction. It is a reduction for the auxiliary arbitrary-coloring one-change problem, not by itself a proof of NORI1 or its universal paired-root condition.

AXIS-FACE NO-GO. Every axis-aligned face of an independent product c box d is itself the independent product of faces of c and d. For a fixed global phase orientation, its rooted phase-signature family therefore remains a Cartesian product, even when that face is selected adaptively according to a prior switch vertex. Thus deletion of axis directions within independently copied colorings cannot generate cross-factor phase constraints. Coupling via nonproduct color dependence, or additional antipodal/root information, would be required for the proposed amplification-then-restriction contradiction.

#### Cyclic sink-component elimination

Let c be antipodally odd on Q_n, K a proper nonempty set of at most seven directions, R its complement. Assume that no direction in K influences an edge rule in R. Then c_R is a legal antipodally odd coloring on Q_R. The full-geodesic profile support and shortest monochromatic antipodal length satisfy W(c)=W(c_R) times F_2^K and ell(c)=ell(c_R)+|K|.

Proof. The established arbitrary-color at-most-one-switch geodesic theorem B_k holds for each k<=7. Fix any antipodal walk P in Q_R from z to bar z and target bits t_i on K. On the lower K-face at exterior vertex z let d_i(u)=c_i(u,z) xor t_i. Choose a K-geodesic with d-word zero^a one^(k-a); reverse the traversal first if necessary. If its zero-block U runs u0 to ua and its one-block is V, the following Q_n antipodal walk has each K-step of color t_i: start at (ua,z), traverse reverse U, follow P with K vertex fixed at u0, and traverse reverse of the full antipodal image of V in the upper K-face. The original zero-block gives c-color t; antipodal complementation makes the one-block give c-color t too. This walk preserves the complete ordered exterior projection P; if P is a full geodesic, the result is a full geodesic.

All R-rules ignore bits in K. Consequently every full c-geodesic projects to one of c_R, and any prescribed profile of c_R together with any K profile is realized by the above construction. Hence W(c)=W(c_R) times F_2^K. Likewise, any monochromatic antipodal c-path projects to a monochromatic antipodal walk of c_R with at least ell(c_R) exterior steps, and it has at least |K| new steps. For the reverse bound, choose a shortest monochromatic c_R-antipodal path as P and prescribe all K colors equal to its color. The constructed antipodal c-walk is monochromatic of length ell(c_R)+|K|. Loop-erasure and the lower bound prove the length identity. Minority defect, profile-support deficit and detour thus persist.

If every strongly connected component in the directed influence graph has size <=7, repeatedly remove a sink SCC by the theorem. The final SCC has size <=7, where the established finite NORI theorem implies all direction-profile targets are realized: recolor any direction according to a prescribed target and take a monochromatic path; antipodal reflection provides both constant colors. Back-substituting the profile cylinders gives W(c)=F_2^n for the original coloring. In particular, every NORI1 counterexample has an SCC of size >=8. Every sink SCC of a minimum-dimensional counterexample has size >=8, because otherwise deletion produces a smaller counterexample.

##### Branching-sparse sink sets of unbounded size

Let c be legal and K a nonempty sink set in its directed influence graph, with R=[n]\K nonempty. Put H={i in K: i influences at least two different direction rules}, L=K\H. Assume |H|<=7; no bound on |K|. Then W(c)=W(c_R) times F_2^K and ell(c)=ell(c_R)+|K|.

Single-edge repair lemma: If an antipodal walk uses direction i once and every out-neighbor of i also occurs at most once, and i has at most one out-neighbor j, its i-step can be assigned either color while retaining all other traversed edge colors. If j precedes i, move i to the last step, otherwise to the first. This crosses no direction whose color rule depends on bit i. For first i, replace root x, order (i,sigma) by root bar(x+e_i), order (i,reverse sigma); only the first edge becomes antipodal, the remainder is traversed backwards. For last i, replace root x, order (sigma,i) by root bar x+e_i, order (reverse sigma,i). This toggles only the last edge. Both manipulations preserve antipodality even when exterior directions repeat.

Profile factorization: Start with any full c_R geodesic realizing arbitrary exterior profile w, append each L direction once, and use the established B_k antipodal two-phase bridge on H (size<=7) to prescribe all H edge colors while retaining the ordered exterior skeleton. All R colors stay w, since K has no arcs into R. For each i in L, the only possible out-neighbor lies in K and is traversed once. Apply the single-edge repair lemma to set its profile bit, preserving all previous profile bits. Every (w,t_K) therefore occurs. Conversely every full c-geodesic projects to a full c_R geodesic with unchanged R colors.

Metric identity: The projection lower bound gives ell(c)>=ell(c_R)+|K|. Start from a shortest monochromatic R antipodal path, append the L steps once, prescribe color zero on H by the B_k bridge (allowing repeated R directions), then set each L step to zero using the same individual repair. R-edge colors are unchanged. This yields a monochromatic antipodal walk of length ell(c_R)+|K|, and loop-erasure proves equality.

Corollary: Every sink strongly connected component in a minimum-dimensional NORI1 counterexample must have at least eight directions with at least two outgoing influence neighbors. Otherwise this theorem deletes it and yields a smaller counterexample. A directed cycle of any length is therefore an eliminable sink component.

**Whole-graph case.** If the influence graph has a single strongly connected component, the sink set is not proper and cannot be deleted. The earlier low-outdegree profile-cylinder theorem and seven-direction prescription theorem nonetheless force at least eight branching directions in any bad coloring. The corollary for every sink SCC of a minimum counterexample uses this separate argument in the one-component case.


##### Acyclic sandwich prescription and single-feedback forcing

Let \(c\) be any legal antipodally odd coloring on \(Q_n\). Its directed influence graph has \(j\to i\) when \(\partial_jc_i\) is nonzero somewhere. Let \(I\subseteq[n]\) induce an acyclic influence graph, let \(J=[n]\setminus I\), and choose a topological order \(i_1,\ldots,i_m\) of \(I\).

**Theorem A (full rootwise prescription on acyclic directions).** For every root \(x\), every target bit vector \(t_I\), and every chosen ordering of \(J\), there is a full antipodal geodesic from \(x\) whose colors in directions \(I\) are \(t_I\). Thus
\[
\boxed{\mathcal W_x(c)|_I=\mathbb F_2^I,\qquad
|\mathcal W_x(c)|\ge2^{|I|}.}\tag{FVS-A}
\]
In particular, for directed feedback vertex number \(\tau\), every root realizes at least \(2^{n-\tau}\) different full color profiles.

*Proof.* Let \(B=\{i\in I:c_i(x)=t_i\}\). Traverse \(B\) in reverse topological order, then all of \(J\) in the chosen order, then \(I\setminus B\) in forward topological order. Before a vertex \(i\in B\), no direction on which \(c_i\) depends has been flipped, so the color is \(c_i(x)=t_i\). Before a vertex \(i\in I\setminus B\), every direction on which \(c_i\) depends has been flipped, so antipodal oddness and independence from its own bit give color \(1+c_i(x)=t_i\). Directions that are not incoming influences have no effect on \(c_i\). The word uses all directions once. \(\square\)

**Theorem B (triangular root-state bijection).** For fixed starting bits \(x_J\) and target \(t_I\), put
\[
b_i(x)=1+c_i(x)+t_i,\qquad
y_i=x_i+b_i(x)\quad (i\in I).\tag{FVS-B}
\]
The map \(x_I\mapsto y_I\) is a bijection, and \(y_I\) is the state on the \(I\)-bits immediately before the middle \(J\)-block in the preceding construction.

*Proof.* For \(i=i_k\), the rule \(c_i(x)\) depends only on \(x_J\) and earlier \(I\)-bits \(x_{i_1},\ldots,x_{i_{k-1}}\), because its incoming influences in \(I\) precede it and the rule ignores its own bit. Therefore \(y_{i_k}=x_{i_k}+g_k(x_J,x_{i_1},\ldots,x_{i_{k-1}})\). This triangular map is inverted recursively in topological order. The middle-state identity follows because the initial block flips just those \(i\) having \(b_i=1\). \(\square\)

**Theorem C (one-feedback full-profile theorem and root density).** If \(D(c)-h\) is acyclic for some direction \(h\), then for every desired full color profile \(t\in\mathbb F_2^n\),
\[
\boxed{|\{x:t\in\mathcal W_x(c)\}|\ge2^{n-1}.}\tag{FVS-C}
\]
In particular at least half of all cube vertices start a red full antipodal geodesic, proving NORI1 in this class. This holds for unrestricted nonlinear direction rules and is sharp for every \(n\ge2\).

*Proof.* Apply Theorem B with \(I=[n]\setminus\{h\}\), \(J=\{h\}\). For either value of \(x_h\), the state \(y_I\) before the \(h\)-step runs bijectively through \(\mathbb F_2^{n-1}\) as the other root bits vary. The rule \(c_h\) ignores \(x_h\), while oddness implies \(c_h(y_I+1_I)=1+c_h(y_I)\). Thus half the choices of \(y_I\) give prescribed color \(t_h\) in direction \(h\). Every other direction already has its prescribed color by Theorem A. There are \(2^{n-2}\) such roots for each value of \(x_h\), totaling \(2^{n-1}\). For a single witness, choose either \(y_I=0\) or \(1_I\) to achieve \(t_h\), invert the triangular map, and form the sandwich word. Given the influence order, this requires \(O(n)\) color-rule evaluations.

For sharpness, use \(c_0=x_1,\ c_1=x_0,\ c_i=x_0\) for \(2\le i<n\). Its influence graph becomes acyclic on deleting direction zero. Both directions zero and one can have prescribed colors \(t_0,t_1\) along a full geodesic only if \(x_0+x_1=1+t_0+t_1\), which holds for half the roots. Whenever it holds, put the remaining directions before or after direction zero according to whether their desired color agrees with the currently held bit zero. Thus half the roots, and no more, realize \(t\). \(\square\)

**Large strongly connected nonlinear example.** For \(n\ge6\), set
\[
c_0=M(x_1,x_{n-2},x_{n-1}),\quad c_1=x_0,\quad c_2=x_1,\quad
c_3=M(x_0,x_1,x_2),\quad c_i=x_{i-1}\ (4\le i<n),
\]
where \(M(a,b,c)=ab+ac+bc\). The rules are edge-consistent and odd. Their influence graph contains the directed Hamilton circuit \(0\to1\to\cdots\to n-1\to0\), and so forms one strongly connected component of size \(n\); deleting direction zero leaves an acyclic influence graph. Theorem C gives at least \(2^{n-1}\) successful starting roots even in this nonlinear, non-star, unbounded strongly connected case.

**Limitation for larger feedback sets.** The single middle-block construction need not succeed for feedback sets of size two. On \(Q_3\), take \(I=\{2\}\), \(J=\{0,1\}\), and \(c_0=x_2,\ c_1=1+x_2,\ c_2=x_0\). No fixed \(01\)-face has a red two-edge geodesic because its two direction colors are opposed. Still the root with \(x_0=1,x_2=0\) and direction order \((0,2,1)\) gives an all-red full geodesic. This delineates the reach of the sandwich construction without assuming a further collective-to-single extraction principle.

A direct \(Q_7\) test verified all \(128\cdot32\) fixed-root prescriptions for one induced five-direction acyclic subset, as well as \(64\) red roots out of \(128\) for a nonlinear coloring with one feedback direction.


##### Two-feedback forcing by opposite-color square rigidity and a pivot

Let \(c\) be any legal antipodally odd undirected-edge coloring of \(Q_n\), \(n\ge2\). Assume that there are two directions \(a,b\) such that the induced directed influence graph on \(I=[n]\setminus\{a,b\}\) is acyclic. Fix a topological order \(i_1,\ldots,i_m\) of \(I\).

**Theorem (two-feedback monochromatic closure and full-profile surjectivity).** Every prescribed vector \(t\in\mathbb F_2^n\) occurs as the direction-indexed color profile of some full antipodal geodesic. In particular, a red full antipodal geodesic exists, establishing NORI1 for all legal nonlinear colorings whose directed influence graph has feedback vertex number at most two. The directed influence graph before deletion may be one strongly connected component of unbounded size.

*Proof.* It suffices to find a fully red geodesic: for arbitrary \(t\), replacing the edge color \(c_i\) by \(c_i+t_i\) preserves edge consistency, antipodal oddness, and the entire directed influence graph. Apply the red case to the recolored system.

We use the acyclic sandwich normalization from the preceding theorem. Given a root \(x\), let \(B=\{i\in I:c_i(x)=0\}\), and let \(A=I\setminus B\). Traverse \(B\) in reverse topological order, then directions \(a,b\) in any chosen order, then \(A\) in forward topological order. Every \(I\)-edge is red. For fixed root bits \(x_a,x_b\), the \(I\)-state just before the \(ab\)-block is
\[
y_i=x_i+1+c_i(x)\quad(i\in I).
\tag{FVS-D1}
\]
The map \(x_I\mapsto y_I\) is bijective: each \(c_{i_k}(x)\) depends only on the two fixed \(ab\)-bits and preceding input bits in \(I\), so the equations invert recursively.

**Case 1: one \(ab\)-square has a red two-edge route.** Choose its \(I\)-face position \(y\), its starting \(ab\)-bits \(u\), and a red route with order either \(ab\) or \(ba\). Fix \(x_{ab}=u\) and invert (FVS-D1) to recover \(x_I\). The sandwich word is a red full antipodal geodesic.

**Case 2: no \(ab\)-square has a red two-edge route.** Antipodal oddness carries any blue two-edge route in an \(ab\)-face at position \(y\) to a red route in the antipodal \(ab\)-face at position \(\bar y\). Hence no \(ab\)-face has a monochromatic two-edge route of either color. A square edge-coloring with neither a red nor a blue two-edge route must alternate colors around its four-cycle. It follows that all \(a\)-edges in each face share one color and all \(b\)-edges the opposite color. Therefore
\[
\boxed{c_a(z)=g(z_I),\qquad c_b(z)=1+g(z_I),}\tag{FVS-D2}
\]
with no dependence on the \(a,b\) bits. The function \(g\) is antipodally odd, so \(g(\bar y)=1+g(y)\). Necessarily \(I\ne\varnothing\), and some direction \(k\in I\) and vertex \(y\in\mathbb F_2^I\) satisfy \(g(y+e_k)=1+g(y)\). The same derivative condition holds at \(\bar y\).

Choose any intermediate \(ab\)-bit pair \(u\). If \(c_k(y,u)=1\), replace \((y,u)\) by \((\bar y,\bar u)\); then \(c_k(y,u)=0\) by antipodal oddness, while \(g\) still changes across the direction \(k\). Let \(f=a\) when \(g(y)=0\) and \(f=b\) when \(g(y)=1\), and write \(s\) for the other member of \(\{a,b\}\). Choose the initial \(ab\)-bits \(x_{ab}=u+e_f\). Then direction \(f\) is red at \(I\)-state \(y\), the direction-\(k\) edge at state \((y,u)\) is red, and direction \(s\) is red at \(I\)-state \(y+e_k\), since \(g\) changes across \(k\).

To make all remaining directions red, define a modified triangular map on roots by
\[
y_k=x_k,\qquad y_i=x_i+1+c_i(x)\quad(i\in I\setminus\{k\}).
\tag{FVS-D3}
\]
For fixed \(x_{ab}\), this map is bijective. Indeed, fix \(x_k=y_k\) first; solve the other root bits in the selected topological order, each equation involving only already recovered predecessors in \(I\). Invert (FVS-D3) for the selected \(y\), obtaining a root \(x\).

Now let \(B=\{i\in I\setminus\{k\}:c_i(x)=0\}\) and \(A=I\setminus(B\cup\{k\})\). Traverse the following direction word:
\[
\boxed{(B\text{ in reverse topological order})\,f\,k\,s\,
(A\text{ in forward topological order}).}\tag{FVS-D4}
\]
Before \(f\), the \(I\)-state is \(y\), and after \(f\) the \(ab\)-state is \(u\). Thus the three central edges \(f,k,s\) are red by construction. Each direction \(i\in B\) is red because none of its input directions has been flipped when it is traversed: the earlier topological directions are still unflipped, and \(k,a,b\) have not yet been crossed. Each direction \(i\in A\) is red because all its input directions have already been flipped: the earlier topological directions were used in \(B\) or earlier in \(A\), and \(k,a,b\) have been crossed. Antipodal oddness gives the required red color in this latter case. Every direction occurs once, proving the theorem. \(\square\)

**Constructive cost.** Given the influence topological order and query access to the edge rules, Case 1 can test every \(ab\)-face using \(O(2^{n-2})\) face positions (and four starting corners each), then invert the triangular normalization using \(O(n)\) further evaluations. In Case 2, a pivotal edge of \(g\) can be located using \(O(n)\) queries by comparing \(g\) along any direction-simple path from \(0^I\) to \(1^I\), since these endpoint values differ. Antipodal oddness chooses a red pivot. The modified triangular map then gives a full red geodesic using \(O(n)\) further edge evaluations. No success-density or collective exchange theorem is used.

**Finite independent test.** A separate implementation generated random legal odd nonlinear color rules with all \(I\)-rules constrained only by the stated acyclic influence order and unrestricted \(a,b\)-rules. It reconstructed and checked individual all-red full direction words in dimensions three through eight. The rigid second case was also independently tested on 300 randomly generated instances in each of dimensions three through eight and dimension ten. Every constructed path was verified to traverse all directions once and have only red edges.

**Why the rigidity matters.** The direct sandwich can fail even if a red full geodesic exists; for instance \(c_a=x_k,\ c_b=1+x_k,\ c_k=x_a\) has no red \(ab\)-route in any \(ab\)-face. The pivot word (FVS-D4) repairs this failure by inserting one direction where the complementary helper colors reverse. For larger feedback sets, absence of a monochromatic full face path does not enforce a similarly simple pair of complementary rules. The proved theorem does not claim closure beyond feedback number two.


**Irreducible two-feedback nonlinear witness family.** On six directions \(0,\ldots,5\), define
\[
c_0=M(x_2,x_4,x_5),\quad c_1=x_0,\quad c_2=x_1,\quad
c_3=M(x_5,x_1,x_2),\quad c_4=x_3,\quad c_5=x_4.
\tag{FVS-D5}
\]
The dependency graph contains vertex-disjoint directed triangles \(0\to1\to2\to0\) and \(3\to4\to5\to3\). The majority rules give influence arcs \(1,2\to3\) and \(4,5\to0\), making the full graph strongly connected. Deleting both directions \(0,3\) leaves the acyclic arcs \(1\to2\) and \(4\to5\). The feedback vertex number is therefore two: at least one vertex of each of the two disjoint triangles must be deleted, and the pair \(0,3\) suffices. Both majority rules are nonlinear and antipodally odd; all other rules are unary and odd.

For every \(n\ge6\) one may lengthen the first directed triangle into an arbitrarily long directed cycle by inserting new unary-reader directions along the edge returning to \(0\), and replacing \(x_2\) in the first majority rule by the bit of the final inserted direction. Both disjoint directed cycles survive and the graph remains strongly connected, while deleting \(0,3\) leaves a directed acyclic graph. Thus the two-feedback theorem handles arbitrary large strongly connected nonlinear systems whose minimum feedback number is two and to which the preceding one-feedback theorem does not apply. In the six-direction instance an exhaustive rooted geodesic enumeration found 58 of the 64 vertices supporting red full geodesics, including, for root \(x=1\) (integer bitmask), the red direction word \((0,5,4,3,2,1)\). The enumeration is illustrative only; existence is proved by the theorem above.


**Fiberwise geodesic-count identity for acyclic complements.** In the setting of Theorem A, fix a prescribed complete profile \(t=(t_I,t_J)\). Let \(G_{c,I,J}^{\rm sand}(t)\) count rooted direction orders of the canonical form
\[
(B_x\text{ reversed in topological order})\,\sigma\,
(I\setminus B_x\text{ in forward topological order}),
\]
where \(B_x=\{i\in I:c_i(x)=t_i\}\) and \(\sigma\) ranges over all permutations of \(J\), that realize the prescribed profile \(t\). For each \(y\in Q_I\), let \(c^{\,y}|_J\) be the ordinary induced coloring of the \(J\)-face at fixed \(I\)-state \(y\), and let \(N_{t_J}(c^{\,y}|_J)\) count its rooted full-geodesic orders with profile \(t_J\). Then
\[
\boxed{
G_{c,I,J}^{\rm sand}(t)=\sum_{y\in Q_I}N_{t_J}(c^{\,y}|_J).
}\tag{FVS-D6}
\]
In particular, if even one \(J\)-face has a full geodesic with profile \(t_J\), the ambient cube has a full geodesic with profile \(t\).

*Proof.* For each fixed starting \(J\)-state \(u\), the triangular map \(x_I\mapsto y_I\) from Theorem B is bijective. Every canonical sandwich from \(x=(x_I,u)\) has profile \(t_I\) on \(I\) and traverses \(J\) from \((y_I,u)\) using the chosen permutation \(\sigma\). Thus such a sandwich realizes the full target if and only if the \(J\)-face geodesic from \(u\) in direction order \(\sigma\) realizes \(t_J\). The triangular map gives a bijection between rooted ambient sandwiches and all rooted \(J\)-face geodesics counted in the right side, proving the identity. \(\square\)

The identity holds even though an induced \(J\)-face need not itself be antipodally odd. Therefore lower-dimensional NORI1 cannot be applied directly to an arbitrary induced face; the opposite-face rigidity in the two-feedback theorem is precisely what is needed when every individual \(J\)-face fails the desired profile.


##### Canonical directed-cycle ancestor core

Let K be the direction labels from which a directed influence path reaches a directed cycle, and let S be all other directions. The induced influence graph on S is acyclic, and no influence arrow goes from S into K. Thus the K-direction rules give a legal odd coloring cK independent of S.

**Theorem.** For every root (u,v) in QK times QS, the attained direction-indexed full-geodesic profiles satisfy W_(u,v)(c)=W_u(cK) times F2^S. Hence the favorable roots for every target full profile t form R_t(c)=R_(tK)(cK) times QS. In particular NORI1 holds for c iff it holds for cK, and the fraction of favorable roots is unchanged. K is the unique minimal set whose complement is acyclic and does not influence K.

**Proof.** Projection of a full geodesic onto K gives one inclusion. For the other inclusion, begin with a geodesic on K having any prescribed profile. Insert the directions of S one at a time in topological influence order. Each new direction rule ignores subsequent inserted bits and is odd on the current subcube, so its colors at the endpoints of the current full geodesic differ. Inserting its edge at the suitable endpoint achieves either prescribed new color, while the earlier rules ignore its bit and their colors persist. This works with any fixed initial S-bits. Minimality of K follows because every directed cycle and all its directed ancestors belong to any set with the two claimed graph properties. The complement of K is peeled by successive singleton sink component deletions. Full detail and independent finite checks are in research note note_5284951226306cf15a399152.


**Quantitative one-direction extension identity.** Let d be any legal odd coloring on Q_m, and append one new direction s, leaving old edge rules unchanged and coloring s-edges by an arbitrary odd function h of the old vertex bits. For a full oriented rooted path P in d, let Z_b(P) count its visited vertices z with h(z)=b. If N_t(d) counts oriented rooted full paths with direction-indexed color profile t, then

N_(t,b)(d+) = 2 sum_(P with profile t) Z_b(P).

Indeed every extended path uniquely projects to an old path plus the insertion position of s and its initial s-bit. Both s-bit choices work, and the new edge has color h(z) at its insertion point. The old path runs between antipodes, so h has different values at its endpoints; hence 1<=Z_b(P)<=m. Consequently

2 N_t(d) <= N_(t,b)(d+) <= 2m N_t(d),
and N_(t,0)(d+) + N_(t,1)(d+) = 2(m+1) N_t(d).

Thus the full color-profile root set is lifted as a Cartesian product while oriented witness multiplicities obey a separate explicit insertion-weighted formula. This was checked independently for random legal odd base colorings on Q2, Q3 and Q4, for all roots, color targets and insertion positions.


##### Logarithmic antipodal-face search for the two-feedback theorem

Assume a legal odd coloring has a supplied pair a,b whose deletion leaves acyclic influence on I. There is a deterministic construction of a full red geodesic using O(n) edge-rule queries, improving the exhaustive conditional-face search in the preceding two-feedback proof. For y in Q_I, inspect the ab-square at y and its antipodal square at bar(y). If either has a red two-step route, lift it via the acyclic triangular root normalization. If neither has one, oddness rules out blue two-step routes as well; both squares must be alternating, with direction-a edges of color g(y) and direction-b edges of the opposite color. The antipodal square satisfies g(bar(y))=1+g(y).

Start with endpoints y=0 and z=1_I. If their paired faces are unfavorable, both alternate and g(y) differs from g(z). Repeatedly choose a midpoint m by flipping half the bits separating y,z, test m and bar(m), and either lift a red route found there or keep the half-interval on which g differs. After at most ceil(log2(n-2)) steps, adjacent alternating faces y and y+e_k have different g-values. Choose ab-bits u so c_k(y,u)=0: if the first choice fails, antipodally translate the two faces and u, which complements the k-edge color while preserving the alternating pattern. Let f be the red feedback direction at y and s the other. Then f,k,s is a red three-step path, using initial ab-bits u+e_f. Invert the modified triangular equations x_k=y_k and y_i=x_i+1+c_i(x) for all other i in I. The resulting full direction order is: before-block directions with c_i(x)=0 in reverse topological order; then f,k,s; then the remaining directions with c_i(x)=1 in forward topological order. Every edge is red by the same predecessor-dependence argument as the previous theorem. For n=2 the initial ab-face already contains a red route. The O(n) total query bound includes triangular inversion. It assumes the feedback pair and influence topological order are provided, not discovered from a black-box oracle.

Independent implementations tested 400 random legal odd acyclic-complement inputs in every dimension 3 through 7 and 60 in dimensions 8 through 10; all returned words were fully verified. An additional 100 trials in every dimension 3 through 10 forced all ab-faces to be alternating, so that the pivot branch was mandatory; all succeeded. This is a constructive speedup of the proved feedback-two theorem, not a new bounded-class extension.


##### Independent incidence realization on interaction trees

Let \(f\) be an arbitrary binary coloring of the undirected edges of \(Q_d\). For each dimension \(i\), write \(f_i(x)\) for the color of the direction-\(i\) edge incident with \(x\); this is independent of \(x_i\). Its **interaction graph** \(G(f)\) joins \(i,j\) when either \(\partial_j f_i\) or \(\partial_i f_j\) is nonzero. Consequently \(f_i\) depends only on the bits of the neighboring directions \(N_G(i)\).

For every incident pair of graph vertices \(i,j\), regard \(a_{ij}\in\mathbb F_2\) as a prescribed value of bit \(j\) at the instant a full direction-simple path traverses dimension \(i\). Let \(\pi\) be the order of the traversed dimensions. The incidence equation is
\[
\boxed{a_{ij}=x_j+[\pi(j)<\pi(i)]\pmod2.}
\tag{1}
\]

**Lemma 1 (universal realization of prescribed incidences on trees).** Let \(T\) be any tree on a set of \(m\ge2\) directions. Prescribe the two incidence bits \(a_{ij},a_{ji}\) independently for every edge \(ij\) of \(T\). There exist an initial cube vertex \(x\) and a permutation \(\pi\) of the directions satisfying every equation (1). In fact, there are two antipodal choices of \(x\), with corresponding reverse orientations of \(T\). A suitable pair can be constructed in linear time from the incidence data.

*Proof.* Choose a tree root \(r\) and set \(x_r\) arbitrarily. Process the tree outward. When the parent \(p\) has known bit \(x_p\) and \(c\) is a new child, orient the edge \(p\to c\) if
\[
\varepsilon_{pc}=a_{cp}+x_p=1,
\]
and orient it \(c\to p\) otherwise. In either case define
\[
x_c=a_{pc}+1+\varepsilon_{pc}\pmod2.
\]
If \(p\) is earlier, its bit at the traversal of \(c\) is \(x_p+1=a_{cp}\); if it is later, the bit is \(x_p=a_{cp}\). The definition of \(x_c\) similarly makes the bit of \(c\) at traversal of \(p\) equal \(a_{pc}\). Thus the incidence equations hold on the new edge. Repeat for all edges. Every orientation of a tree is acyclic, so it extends to a total permutation \(\pi\). Changing \(x_r\) flips all inferred root bits and reverses every tree-edge orientation, giving the second solution. QED.

**Theorem 2 (admissible monochromatic targets on arbitrary nonlinear trees).** Suppose the interaction graph \(G(f)\) is a tree and choose a prescribed color \(t\in\{0,1\}\) **attained by every direction's local neighbor-bit function**:
\[
\boxed{t\in\bigcap_{i\in V(G)}\operatorname{im}(f_i).}
\]
Then there exists a full dimension-simple antipodal geodesic of constant color \(t\). The statement holds for arbitrary nonlinear local functions and is constructive.

*Proof.* For each \(i\), the displayed hypothesis permits an independent assignment \((a_{ij})_{j\in N(i)}\) satisfying \(f_i((a_{ij})_j)=t\). Lemma 1 realizes all chosen incidence bits simultaneously through a root and an acyclic orientation of the tree; topologically order its vertices to obtain a full antipodal geodesic. Every traversed edge has color \(t\). QED.

**Necessary qualification.** Connectedness of the *undirected* interaction graph alone does not imply that each \(f_i\) is nonconstant. An edge \(ij\) can arise solely from dependence of \(f_j\) on bit \(i\), while \(f_i\) is constant. For example on \(Q_3\) let \(f_1\equiv0\), \(f_3\equiv1\), and \(f_2(x)=x_1+x_3\). The interaction graph is the connected path \(1-2-3\), but no monochromatic full geodesic can exist, because every full geodesic uses direction 1 of color zero and direction 3 of color one. Thus the previously published unrestricted monochromatic-tree claim was false; the theorem above replaces it.

**Corollary 3 (paired roots in target-admissible interaction forests).** Suppose \(G(f)\) is a forest with \(c\) nontrivial connected tree components and \(r\) isolated vertices. Assume that in each nontrivial component \(C\), there is a bit \(t_C\) attained by **every** local color function in \(C\). Then
\[
\boxed{|P(f)|\ge 2^{c+r}.}
\]
In particular the condition holds when all local functions in each nontrivial component are nonconstant.

*Proof.* Theorem 2 produces a monochromatic color-\(t_C\) antipodal geodesic in each component; reversing it gives a second root at its antipode. An isolated direction has a constant color and allows either root bit. Select the roots independently in all components. To form a \(0^*1^*\) full geodesic, concatenate all component paths and singleton directions colored zero, followed by those colored one. For the reverse \(1^*0^*\) orientation, concatenate the same selected component paths in the opposite color-block order. Independence between interaction components preserves all edge colors and all dimensions are used once. The choices give at least \(2^{c+r}\) paired roots. QED.

**Corollary 4 (NORI1 over target-admissible forest facets).** An antipodally odd coloring of \(Q_{d+1}=Q_d\times\{0,1\}\) whose lower-facet interaction forest satisfies the common-target condition of Corollary 3 admits at least \(2^{c+r}\) distinct directed monochromatic full antipodal geodesics, for arbitrary odd vertical bridge colors.

*Proof.* Apply Corollary 3 and the universal paired-root bridge equivalence. QED.

##### Cycle-syndrome criterion for arbitrary interaction graphs

The tree realization proof extends to a graph with cycles, but now two precisely described obstructions arise.

For an arbitrary undirected graph \(G\) on the direction set and a full specification of the incident bits \(a_{ij}\) on its edges, set
\[
\lambda_{ij}=1+a_{ij}+a_{ji}\pmod2
\tag{3}
\]
for each edge \(ij\).

**Theorem 5 (cycle parity and acyclic orientation characterization).** The incidence prescription (1) is realizable by a root \(x\) and a total direction order \(\pi\) if and only if the following two conditions hold:

(i) for every cycle \(C\) of \(G\),
\[
\boxed{\sum_{ij\in E(C)}\lambda_{ij}=0\pmod2;}
\tag{4}
\]

(ii) choose either vertex potential \(x\) solving \(x_i+x_j=\lambda_{ij}\) on each connected component, and orient every graph edge \(j\to i\) when \(a_{ij}+x_j=1\); the resulting graph orientation is acyclic.

When (i) holds, the solutions for \(x\) are the two global-complement choices on each connected component. Replacing a potential by its complement reverses every edge orientation in that component, so condition (ii) is independent of which potential is chosen.

*Proof.* If (1) holds for some \(x,\pi\), summing the two incidence equations at the endpoints of an edge gives
\[
a_{ij}+a_{ji}=x_i+x_j+1.
\]
Thus the \(\lambda\)-values form a vertex coboundary, which is equivalent to (4). The induced edge orientations follow the total order \(\pi\) and hence are acyclic.

Conversely (4) makes the edge equations \(x_i+x_j=\lambda_{ij}\) solvable, uniquely up to one bit per connected component. Orient edge \(j\to i\) whenever \(a_{ij}+x_j=1\). Since
\[
(a_{ij}+x_j)+(a_{ji}+x_i)
=a_{ij}+a_{ji}+\lambda_{ij}=1,
\]
this assigns one direction to each undirected graph edge. If the orientation is acyclic, choose any of its topological total orders \(\pi\). The incidence equations (1) hold by construction. Replacing all \(x_i\) in one component by \(x_i+1\) reverses each orientation there; directed cycles exist in an orientation if and only if they exist in its reversal. QED.

**Corollary 6 (cyclomatic localization of a monochromatic obstruction).** If local neighbor-bit inputs making every direction color \(t\) can be chosen independently, then failure to realize those inputs as a monochromatic full geodesic can arise only from the cycle-parity constraints (4) and the acyclicity requirement in Theorem 5. A graph with cycle-space dimension
\[
\beta_1(G)=|E(G)|-|V(G)|+\#\text{components}
\]
has \(\beta_1(G)\) independent parity equations. On a forest there are none and the orientation condition is automatic. This gives a cycle-rank parameterization of the remaining difficulty, preserving all direction uses.

**Example 7 (a single even cycle already obstructs monochromaticity).** On \(Q_{2r}\), \(r\ge2\), index dimensions cyclically and define
\[
f_i(x)=x_{i-1}+x_{i+1}+a_i\pmod2,
\qquad \sum_i a_i=1\pmod2.
\tag{5}
\]
Its interaction graph is the even cycle \(C_{2r}\). Along any full antipodal dimension order, each graph edge contributes once to the sum of the traversed colors, while every starting bit appears twice. Therefore
\[
\sum_{\text{all }2r\text{ steps}}\text{color}
=\sum_i a_i+|E(C_{2r})|
=1\pmod2.
\]
A monochromatic word of even length has parity zero, so this coloring has **no monochromatic full antipodal geodesic from any root**. This shows that the tree monochromatic theorem does not extend unchanged to unicyclic interaction graphs. The paired-root conjecture remains a different and weaker assertion: existence of both monotone orientations from one root is not ruled out by this parity obstruction.

**Closure program.** Theorem 5 isolates the first obstruction after constructing admissible local tree prescriptions: nonzero syndrome around independent cycles and directed circuits of an induced orientation. To extend a closure proof toward general interactions, one should seek simultaneous prescribed input patterns supporting the two monotone orientations and show that a minimal incompatible cycle can be repaired by changing the seam placement or by an exchange of path orders. Unlike a bound based on small cube dimensions, the present realization and obstruction calculus applies to graphs of arbitrary order and arbitrary nonlinear local coloring functions.### Quantitative tree incidence paths

For a connected nontrivial interaction tree \(T\), let
\[
r_i(t)=|\{a\in\mathbb F_2^{N(i)}:f_i(a)=t\}|\ge1.
\]
Let \(G_t(f)\) be the number of directed rooted full antipodal geodesics of constant color \(t\).

**Theorem 8 (tree path census).** For each \(t\in\{0,1\}\),
\[
\boxed{G_t(f)\ge2\prod_i r_i(t).}
\tag{6}
\]
Indeed, if \(\mathcal A_t=\prod_i f_i^{-1}(t)\), and \(O(a)\) is the oriented tree resulting from the incidence-realization lemma with root bit fixed, while \(L(O)\) counts its topological total orders, then
\[
\boxed{G_t(f)=2\sum_{a\in\mathcal A_t}L(O(a)).}
\tag{7}
\]

*Proof.* For each local-successful incidence specification \(a\), the tree realization lemma supplies two antipodal initial vertices. Their tree orientations are reversals and have equal numbers of topological orders. Each topological order traverses every dimension once, realizing the specified neighbor-bit inputs and therefore constant edge color \(t\). Conversely each such rooted monochromatic path determines its local incidence specification, so paths from different specifications cannot coincide. Summation gives (7), and \(L(O)\ge1\) gives (6). QED.

**Corollary 9 (balanced nonlinear trees).** If each local color function gives color \(t\) on half of its neighbor assignments, then
\[
G_t(f)\ge2^{d-1},
\]
since \(\sum_i(\deg_T(i)-1)=d-2\). There is no linearity assumption.

##### Affine parity colorings on one interaction cycle

Index the \(n\ge3\) directions cyclically. Define
\[
\boxed{f_i(x)=a_i+x_{i-1}+x_{i+1}\pmod2,}
\tag{8}
\]
and write \(A=\sum_i a_i\pmod2\). Fix a root \(x\) and let \(b_i=a_i+x_{i-1}+x_{i+1}\), so \(\sum_i b_i=A\). If a direction permutation orients each cycle edge from earlier to later, with \(p_i\) the parity of the number of earlier neighbors of \(i\), then its step color in direction \(i\) is \(b_i+p_i\).

**Lemma 10 (acyclic cycle indegree parity).** A vector \(p\in\mathbb F_2^n\) arises as the indegree-parity vector of an acyclic orientation of \(C_n\) if and only if
\[
\boxed{\sum_i p_i=n\pmod2,\qquad p\ne\mathbf1.}
\tag{9}
\]
When the parity equation holds there are two orientations having those parities, related by reversal of every cycle edge; they are both cyclic precisely for \(p=\mathbf1\).

*Proof.* Let \(u_i=1\) if \(i\) precedes \(i+1\) on their graph edge. Then
\(p_i=1+u_{i-1}+u_i\pmod2\).
Summing gives the parity condition. If it holds, choosing one \(u_i\) freely determines all the others around the cycle, with two complementary solutions. An orientation of a simple cycle is cyclic precisely when all its graph edges point around the cycle consistently; this makes \(p_i=1\) at every vertex. Every other orientation admits a total topological ordering. QED.

**Theorem 11 (full paired-root classification for cycle-neighbor parity colorings).**
\[
\boxed{|P(f)|=\begin{cases}2^n,&n\text{ even},\\2^n-2,&n\text{ odd}.\end{cases}}
\tag{10}
\]
More precisely:
(a) If \(n\) is even and \(A=0\), every root supports a monochromatic full geodesic.
(b) If \(n\) is even and \(A=1\), no root supports a monochromatic full geodesic, yet every root supports both color words \(0^{n-1}1\) and \(10^{n-1}\).
(c) If \(n\) is odd, every root except two antipodal roots supports a monochromatic full geodesic of color \(1+A\); those two exceptional roots admit no monotone full color word.

*Proof.* Suppose \(n\) is even. If \(A=0\), the parity vector \(p=b\) meets Lemma 10's sum condition. If \(b\ne\mathbf1\), its acyclic orientation gives all-zero traversed edge colors. If \(b=\mathbf1\), take \(p=\mathbf0\) instead, giving all-one traversed colors. Hence every root is paired.

If \(n\) is even and \(A=1\), then \(b\) has odd Hamming parity. Choose \(v\) with \(b_v=1\) and prescribe the traversed color of direction \(v\) to be one and all others zero. The required indegree parity is \(p=b+e_v\), whose total parity is zero and whose value at \(v\) is zero. The two opposite acyclic orientations from Lemma 10 make \(v\) respectively a source (indegree zero) and a sink (indegree two). Extend the first to a topological order with \(v\) first, and the second to one with \(v\) last. These give the two required words from the **same root**. No constant-color word is possible: every full path has total color parity
\(\sum_i b_i+\sum_i p_i=A+n=1\), while any constant word of even length has parity zero.

Now suppose \(n\) is odd. Let \(t=1+A\). To obtain a constant color-\(t\) path, the desired indegree parity is \(p=b+t\), with sum \(A+nt=A+t=1=n\pmod2\). Lemma 10 therefore gives a suitable acyclic orientation unless \(p=\mathbf1\), equivalently \(b_i=A\) at every direction. The exceptional roots solve
\[
x_{i-1}+x_{i+1}=A+a_i\pmod2
\quad\text{for all }i.
\]
The right side sums to zero; the linear map \(x\mapsto(x_{i-1}+x_{i+1})_i\) on an odd cycle has kernel consisting of the two constant binary strings, because kernel elements have period two and \(n\) is odd. Thus precisely two antipodal roots are exceptional.

At either exceptional root \(b_i=A\) for every \(i\). Along any full direction order the first step has no earlier graph neighbors and the last has two, so their colors both equal \(A\). A monotone binary word with equal first and last entries must be constant \(A\). But total step-color parity is \(\sum_i b_i+\sum_i p_i=A+1\), whereas the constant word \(A^n\) has parity \(A\). Thus no monotone full path exists from either exceptional root. This proves the theorem. QED.

**Closure implication.** The first cycle-parity obstruction to a monochromatic full geodesic is sometimes unavoidable: case (b) rules out such a path in every even dimension. Nevertheless the obstruction can be moved between the first and last directions by reversing a cycle orientation, yielding the paired paths NORI1 requires at every root. This identifies an induction motif beyond the tree-realization theorem but does not settle nonlinear cyclic interactions.

#### Pendant direction elimination by a two-word insertion lemma

The tree realization theorem resolves interaction forests, but a stronger property is available: a responsive pendant direction can be removed from **any** interaction graph, regardless of the complexity of the remaining graph.

Let \(f\) color the edges of \(Q_{m+1}\), with a distinguished direction \(i\) and another direction \(j\ne i\). Assume
\[
f_i(x)=x_j+a\quad(a\in\mathbb F_2)
\tag{11}
\]
for every direction-\(i\) edge, and assume that for all directions \(k\notin\{i,j\}\), the color \(f_k\) is independent of bit \(x_i\). The color \(f_j\) may depend **arbitrarily** on \(x_i\) and all other permitted bits. These assumptions hold whenever \(i\) is a leaf of the undirected interaction graph and its own color function depends nontrivially on the bit of its neighbor \(j\). Let \(f^{(0)},f^{(1)}\) denote the facet colorings obtained by fixing \(x_i=0,1\).

**Theorem 12 (responsive-leaf paired-root lifting).** Under (11), every root \(x\in P(f^{(0)})\) has at least one lift among \((x,0),(x,1)\) belonging to \(P(f)\). The same conclusion holds with the facet \(x_i=1\) in place of \(x_i=0\). Consequently
\[
\boxed{|P(f)|\ge |P(f^{(0)})\cup P(f^{(1)})|
\ge\max(|P(f^{(0)})|,|P(f^{(1)})|).}
\tag{12}
\]
In particular, paired-root existence is preserved by adjoining a responsive pendant direction, even when the interaction between that leaf and its neighbor is bidirectional.

*Proof.* Fix \(x\in P(f^{(0)})\), and select complete facet geodesics \(P_\uparrow,P_\downarrow\) from \(x\) with color words \(0^*1^*\) and \(1^*0^*\). Let \(u\) be the color of direction \(j\) on \(P_\uparrow\), and \(v\) its color on \(P_\downarrow\). Put
\[
\alpha=x_j+a,\qquad\beta=1+\alpha.
\tag{13}
\]
If the new \(i\)-step is inserted **after** the \(j\)-step into either facet path, start the enlarged path with \(x_i=0\). All old step colors remain unchanged: direction \(j\) is traversed while \(x_i=0\), and the colors of all other old directions are independent of \(x_i\). The inserted \(i\)-edge then has color \(\beta\), because the \(j\)-bit has been toggled. Inserting a bit \(\beta\) after direction \(j\) preserves the nondecreasing word if \(\beta=1\) or \(u=0\); it preserves the nonincreasing word if \(\beta=0\) or \(v=1\). When \(\beta=1\), place the inserted step at the end of the nondecreasing path and immediately after \(j\) in the nonincreasing path (provided \(v=1\)). When \(\beta=0\), put it immediately after \(j\) in the nondecreasing path (provided \(u=0\)) and at the end of the nonincreasing path.

Alternatively, insert the new \(i\)-step **before** direction \(j\) and start at \(x_i=1\). Again all old colors are read from facet zero. The inserted step has color \(\alpha\), since \(j\) is still unused. Such insertion preserves the nondecreasing word when \(\alpha=0\) or \(u=1\), and preserves the nonincreasing word when \(\alpha=1\) or \(v=0\), placing the new step at the beginning or immediately before \(j\) as appropriate.

Now \(\alpha+\beta=1\). If \(\alpha=0,\beta=1\), the after-\(j\) construction works when \(v=1\), and the before-\(j\) construction works when \(v=0\). If \(\alpha=1,\beta=0\), the after-\(j\) construction works when \(u=0\), and the before-\(j\) construction works when \(u=1\). Thus one starting \(i\)-bit always supports both monotone words from the same enlarged root. All steps remain dimension-simple. This proves the first assertion; interchanging the two facets gives the same argument for \(f^{(1)}\).

For every \(x\) in the union of the two facet paired-root sets, choose one successful enlarged root in its two-element \(i\)-fiber. Different \(x\) give different roots, proving (12). QED.

**Corollary 13 (responsive-leaf pruning of irreducible obstructions).** Starting with any cube-edge coloring, repeatedly remove a leaf direction \(i\) of its undirected interaction graph whenever \(f_i\) depends nontrivially on its unique neighbor. At each removal restrict to either chosen facet of \(i\). If the final lower-dimensional coloring has a paired root, then the initial coloring also has a paired root. In particular the terminal coloring may be resolved by any previously proved criterion, including the corrected target-admissible forest theorem, the star theorem, or directed influence component seam lifting. Every hypothetical paired-root counterexample remains a counterexample under either facet restriction at every responsive pendant direction.

*Proof.* Theorem 12 lifts paired roots from either facet; contraposition and iteration prove the last assertion. QED.

**Proposition 14 (residual constant-source leaf obstruction).** Suppose instead the pendant direction \(i\) has constant edge color \(t\in\{0,1\}\), while its sole neighbor \(j\) may depend on bit \(i\), and all other old direction colors are independent of \(i\). Fix a paired root \(x\) of facet zero. If either of its two monotone witness paths traverses direction \(j\) with color \(t\), then at least one of \((x,0),(x,1)\) is paired in the full cube.

*Proof.* In the preceding insertion argument, now \(\alpha=\beta=t\). If \(t=0\) and the nondecreasing witness has its \(j\)-step colored zero, insert \(i\) after \(j\) when starting at \(i=0\); append \(i\) to the nonincreasing witness. If the nonincreasing witness has its \(j\)-step colored zero, insert \(i\) before \(j\) when starting at \(i=1\), and prepend it to the nondecreasing witness. The two cases for \(t=1\) follow by interchanging the colors and orientations. Old colors again remain unchanged because direction \(j\) is traversed in facet zero. QED.

Thus, for a constant-color pendant direction to obstruct this elementary lifting construction, **every** monotone facet witness at **every** paired root must traverse its neighboring direction with the opposite color. This gives a precise rigidity condition for the remaining source-leaf case, which is not settled by the responsive-leaf theorem.

**Connection to closure.** The directed SCC theorem removes one-way dependence blocks, while Theorem 12 eliminates bidirectionally interacting pendant directions with a nonconstant leaf function. Together they show that a minimal counterexample cannot be explained solely by a large strongly connected component with responsive trees attached to it. The unresolved leaf obstruction is asymmetric: a constant-colored leaf influencing its neighbor, rather than a leaf whose own color responds to that neighbor.

#### Source-pendant directions and the one-class cross-favorability bottleneck

Let \(f\) be any binary coloring of \(Q_{m+1}=Q_m\times\{0,1\}\) whose edges in the added direction \(i\) all have the same color \(t\). No other hypothesis is imposed initially. Let \(h_0,h_1\) be the induced colorings of the two \(m\)-dimensional facets.

**Lemma 15 (constant-direction cross-seam gluing).** If either of the two intersections
\[
\boxed{A_0(h_0)\cap A_1(h_1),\qquad
A_0(h_1)\cap A_1(h_0)}
\tag{14}
\]
is nonempty, then the full coloring \(f\) has a paired root.

*Proof.* Suppose \(z\in A_0(h_0)\cap A_1(h_1)\). If \(t=0\), start at \((z,1)\). A nondecreasing full path traverses the new direction first (color zero) and then follows the chosen \(0^*1^*\) path in facet zero. A nonincreasing full path follows the chosen \(1^*0^*\) path in facet one and then traverses the new direction last (color zero). Both begin at the same root, are dimension-simple and monotone. If \(t=1\), start instead at \((z,0)\): the nondecreasing path follows its facet-zero path first and then uses the new direction last (color one), whereas the nonincreasing path uses the new direction first and then follows its facet-one path. The other intersection in (14) is handled by interchanging the two facets. QED.

**Corollary 16 (two-sided cross separation forced by a bad source leaf).** If \(f\) has no paired root and its direction-\(i\) edges have constant color, both intersections in (14) must be empty.

If, in addition, \(i\) is a leaf of the undirected interaction graph with sole neighbor \(j\), then \(h_0,h_1\) differ only in the colors of the edges of direction \(j\); every other direction has the same colors in both facets. Thus a bad constant-source pendant direction forces a pair of colorings with **one direction-class difference** whose opposite-orientation feasible-root sets are mutually disjoint.

**Theorem 17 (necessary structure of a minimum-dimension counterexample).** Suppose the paired-root conjecture fails and choose a counterexample \(f\) of least cube dimension \(d\). Then:

1. Every proper facet coloring has a paired root, by minimum-dimensional choice.
2. The undirected interaction graph is connected, by Cartesian product factorization.
3. The interaction graph cannot satisfy the common-local-target hypothesis of corrected Theorem 2, since such a coloring would have a monochromatic geodesic and hence a paired root. It is **not proved** that a connected interaction forest always has paired roots without that hypothesis.
4. Every pendant direction \(i\), if present, has a **constant** edge color. Otherwise responsive-leaf lifting would produce a paired root from a lower-dimensional facet.
5. For each constant-colored pendant direction with neighbor \(j\), the two lower-dimensional facet colorings differ only on direction \(j\); they each have paired roots but their two cross-orientation feasible-root intersections vanish.
6. Its directed influence graph has a strongly connected component of size at least four by seam lifting, or at least five using the separate computer-assisted four-cube certificate.

*Proof.* The cited factorization, conditional tree, pendant lifting, and seam theorems prove the assertions. The earlier statement that connectedness and badness force an undirected graph cycle depended on the incorrect unrestricted forest claim and has been withdrawn. QED.

**Proposed sufficient closure lemma (open).** Let \(g,h\) be two arbitrary binary colorings of \(Q_m\) that **agree on every edge outside one direction class**. Prove
\[
\boxed{A_0(g)\cap A_1(h)\ne\varnothing.}
\tag{15}
\]
This is considerably narrower than demanding cross-favorability for two completely unrelated colorings. If established for every \(m\), Lemma 15 and Theorem 12 would rule out all pendant directions in a least-dimension paired-root counterexample, leaving an undirected interaction graph of minimum degree at least two. Moreover the theorem would make *all* constant-source pendant directions safely removable, complementing the responsive-leaf elimination theorem.

**Additional implication.** If either facet coloring \(h_s\) of a constant-source leaf has a paired root with a monochromatic full path of the same color \(t\) as the leaf, that path lifts to a monochromatic full path of the full cube: start in facet \(s\), retain every old direction's edge colors by taking the constant new direction at the suitable end while the sole neighbor is read in facet \(s\), and append the same-color step. In particular the failure certificates above require careful attention to the one-switch witnesses, not merely the existence of independently monochromatic facet paths of the favorable color.

The unresolved source-leaf obstruction has thus been isolated as a one-direction cross-intersection problem, while responsive leaves have been removed unconditionally. This provides a focused next target for root-synchronization or path-exchange arguments.

#### Local-incidence enumeration of arbitrary full geodesic color words

The cycle-syndrome theorem can be sharpened to describe *all* rooted full geodesics and both monotone orientations as local incidence constraints, with no restriction to trees, affine color functions, or special orders.

Let \(G=G(f)\) be a connected interaction graph on the \(d\) cube directions, and let
\[
f_i:\mathbb F_2^{N_G(i)}\to\mathbb F_2
\]
be its arbitrary local direction-color functions. Fix any prescribed direction-indexed step-color vector \(t=(t_i)_{i\in V(G)}\in\mathbb F_2^d\). Define the independently selectable local input patterns
\[
\mathcal A(t)=\prod_{i\in V(G)} f_i^{-1}(t_i).
\tag{16}
\]
For \(a\in\mathcal A(t)\), put \(\lambda_{ij}=1+a_{ij}+a_{ji}\) on each graph edge. If \(\lambda\) has zero sum around every cycle, choose either solution \(x\) of \(x_i+x_j=\lambda_{ij}\), orient graph edge \(j\to i\) when \(a_{ij}+x_j=1\), and denote the resulting orientation by \(O(a,x)\). The other root potential is \(\bar x\), which reverses the entire orientation.

Let \(L(O)\) be the number of topological total orders of an acyclic graph orientation \(O\), and zero when \(O\) has a directed cycle. Let \(L_\uparrow(O,t)\) count those topological total orders \(\pi\) that also satisfy
\[
t_{\pi_1}\le t_{\pi_2}\le\cdots\le t_{\pi_d},
\]
and define \(L_\downarrow(O,t)\) similarly with reversed inequality.

**Theorem 18 (local incidence path census).** The number of rooted directed full cube geodesics whose edge color in direction \(i\) is \(t_i\) equals
\[
\boxed{
N_t(f)=\sum_{\substack{a\in\mathcal A(t)\\
\lambda(a)\text{ has zero cycle periods}}}
\Bigl(L(O(a,x))+L(O(a,x)^{\rm rev})\Bigr).
}
\tag{17}
\]
The corresponding number whose *ordered* step colors are nondecreasing, respectively nonincreasing, is obtained by replacing \(L\) with \(L_\uparrow(O,t)\), respectively \(L_\downarrow(O,t)\), in both summands.

*Proof.* A rooted geodesic with root \(x\) and direction order \(\pi\) yields the incidence inputs
\(a_{ij}=x_j+[\pi(j)<\pi(i)]\).
Its color in direction \(i\) is \(f_i((a_{ij})_j)=t_i\), so its incidence specification lies in \(\mathcal A(t)\). As in Theorem 5, the resulting edge cochain \(\lambda\) is a vertex coboundary and the induced graph orientation is acyclic, with \(\pi\) among its topological extensions.

Conversely, for any \(a\) with zero cycle periods, the two root potentials \(x,\bar x\) give opposite graph orientations. Each topological extension of either orientation realizes the same prescribed incident bit values at all direction steps. Its color vector is therefore \(t\). Distinct incidence specifications cannot represent the same rooted order, because the latter determines every \(a_{ij}\). Summing counts every rooted geodesic once and gives (17). Restricting the counted topological extensions to color-sorted orders proves the monotone versions. QED.

**Corollary 19 (monotone path criterion by an oriented graph cut).** Given an incidence choice \(a\in\mathcal A(t)\) with vanishing cycle periods, a rooted full \(0^*1^*\) geodesic with step-color vector \(t\) is represented by one of its two potentials if and only if its induced orientation is acyclic **and every edge between a vertex with \(t_i=0\) and one with \(t_j=1\) points from the zero vertex toward the one vertex**. For a \(1^*0^*\) path, reverse the direction of all cross-color edges.

*Proof.* A topological order that first lists all vertices of color zero and then all of color one exists if and only if the orientation has no directed cycle and no edge pointing from a one-labeled vertex toward a zero-labeled vertex. Under these conditions, take a topological order of the zero-induced subgraph followed by one of the one-induced subgraph. The reverse-color assertion is analogous. QED.

**Corollary 20 (topological reduction of the paired-root requirement).** A root \(x\) is paired precisely when there are two locally successful incidence patterns \(a^\uparrow,a^\downarrow\) (possibly having different step-color vectors \(t^\uparrow,t^\downarrow\)), both inducing *the same root potential \(x\)*, whose graph orientations are acyclic and whose respective color cuts point in opposite monotone directions. This is a finite local-incidence formulation of the paired-root problem that retains the full one-use-per-dimension condition.

**Structural significance.** Tree interaction graphs have no cycle-period restrictions and every induced orientation is acyclic, explaining Theorem 2. A graph with cycles introduces a graphic-cohomology obstruction \(\lambda\notin B^1(G;\mathbb F_2)\), followed by acyclic-orientation restrictions. The cross-color cut criterion adds a further orientation constraint only when both colors occur. This exposes an intrinsic incidence/chamber object on which a deletion-contraction or cycle-exchange proof may operate, rather than testing small cube orders.

**Relation to existing graph-orientation literature.** The parity part is closely related to the acyclic orientation with prescribed indegree parities problem: see Sylvain Gravier, Matthieu Petiteau, and Isabelle Sivignon, *Some polynomial classes for the acyclic orientation with parity constraint problem*, arXiv:2603.09475 (March 2026), and the EGRES open problem on acyclic orientations with parity constraints. Acyclicity is essential and nontrivial on graphs with many cycles, as illustrated already by complete graphs. The added feature here is that the target parities and color cut can be chosen through the local color-function fibers and that two compatible root certificates are sought, rather than one prescribed parity vector.

#### Unconditional paired-root theorem for arbitrary nonlinear interaction trees

The preceding target-admissible monochromatic-tree theorem is intentionally conditional: opposite constant-colored direction classes prevent monochromatic full paths. Nevertheless **every** tree-local coloring admits both monotone path orientations at one common root. This resolves the source-pendant obstruction for entire interaction trees without requiring monochromatic paths.

Let \(T\) be a tree on the direction set \(V(T)\), and let
\[
f_v:\{0,1\}^{N_T(v)}\to\{0,1\}
\]
